ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Progress Note 4 — Sick Visit — Josephine Baker — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Same-day sick visit for a nosebleed on dual antiplatelet therapy

text.paragraph: Nosebleed this morning that took 25 minutes to stop. [S]

Ms. Baker, a 63-year-old woman who had a heart attack with a stent to the right coronary artery twelve weeks ago, asked for a same-day visit. This morning her left nostril bled for about 25 minutes. She sat forward and pinched the soft part of her nose, as the rehabilitation nurse had shown her, and it stopped; it has not started again. It is the first nosebleed she can remember. The weather has been hot and dry and she has had the windows open at night. She takes aspirin 81 mg and clopidogrel 75 mg and wondered whether she should stop them. She has had no bleeding from the gums, no blood in the urine or stool, no black stools, no easy bruising beyond a small mark on one arm, and no lightheadedness or breathlessness. She has not picked or blown her nose hard and takes no anti-inflammatory pain medicines. [S]

text.paragraph: Vital signs recorded on 1969-06-16; see the Vital Signs section. [S]

tr.td: Well and calm; blood pressure 132/80, pulse 70
Dry, crusted mucosa over the front of the left nasal septum with a small prominent vessel; no active bleeding; right side normal; no posterior bleeding in the throat
No blood in the pharynx; gums normal
One small bruise on the left forearm; no petechiae

Breathlessness on exertion and tiredness since discharge three weeks after the heart attack, without chest pain at rest; cause to be determined (heart function, ischemia, anemia, medicine effect or deconditioning)
S — Synthetic presenting problem, resolved at the second visit when the echocardiogram and cardiology attributed it to ticagrelor.

Coronary artery disease after a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction three weeks before intake, treated with one drug-eluting stent to the right coronary artery; synthetic modern episode linked to the documented heart attack of March 1912
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis; the 1969 heart attack remains D in the history.
High blood pressure, found during the hospital stay for the heart attack
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis; no claim about her real blood pressure.

Absence of the uterus after an emergency hysterectomy at about 35, during a long, grave illness after the loss of a pregnancy; whether the ovaries were removed is not known; counted as a possible early menopause when weighing her cardiovascular risk
S — Synthetic modern status linked to the retrospective account of a hysterectomy in 1941 or 1942; the operation itself rests on one secondary source.
Breathlessness from ticagrelor: a common, harmless side effect, resolved after the change to clopidogrel
S — Synthetic diagnosis at the second visit; resolved at the third visit after the switch.
Raised lipoprotein(a), 172 nmol/L, an inherited risk-enhancing factor
S — Synthetic result measured once at the second visit.
Financial strain: heavy debts after the loss of her home and estate, with income only from performing, which she has stopped while she recovers
S — Synthetic social need anchored to her documented debts and the loss of Les Milandes.
Anterior nosebleed from the left side of the nose, lasting about 25 minutes, in dry weather on aspirin and clopidogrel; stopped with pressure; no further bleeding
S — Synthetic intercurrent problem at an unscheduled visit; it follows from dual antiplatelet therapy and does not echo a documented illness.

Adverse effect of antithrombotic drugs, initial encounter

list.item:
Anterior nosebleed on dual antiplatelet therapy (R04.0). A single anterior nosebleed from dry mucosa over the front of the septum, controlled with first aid. Hemoglobin 11.9 g/dL, little changed from 12.2 at intake, and platelets 258. Blood pressure is at goal. This is a minor bleed and not a reason to stop antiplatelet therapy twelve weeks after a drug-eluting stent, when stopping would raise the risk of stent thrombosis. [S]
Continue aspirin 81 mg and clopidogrel 75 mg; do not stop either without speaking to cardiology.
Saline spray to both nostrils three times a day and petroleum jelly inside the front of the nose at night for two weeks; a humidifier in the bedroom.
If it bleeds again: sit forward, pinch the soft part of the nose firmly for 15 minutes by the clock, and come in or go to the emergency department if it lasts more than 30 minutes.
Cautery only if bleeding recurs from the same vessel.

Coronary artery disease after a stent (I25.10). No angina; rehabilitation going well. [S]
No change in medicines.

text.paragraph: Guideline basis: 2023 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Chronic Coronary Disease (2023); 2025 ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI Guideline for the Management of Patients With Acute Coronary Syndromes (2025); Clinical Practice Guideline: Nosebleed (Epistaxis) (2020)

Follow-up: Nurse telephone call in two days. Twelve-week review in five weeks as planned. Return the same day for bleeding that lasts more than 30 minutes, black stools or lightheadedness; call 911 for chest pain. Next scheduled visit 1969-07-21: twelve-week review: exercise test, lipids, mood, and the return to performing. [S]
